power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.current_review_stage:
The project is currently in the manuscript preparation stage. The review team completed the PROSPERO registration form and attempted to submit the protocol prospectively, prior to completing screening. We subsequently discovered that the registration had not been completed successfully. After identifying this issue, we returned to PROSPERO and repeated the submission process in order to determine why the original registration had not been completed. This second attempt similarly did not reach the final confirmation stage, clarifying that the original submission had not been successfully registered. By this time, the review had progressed substantially and data analysis had begun.

We therefore elected to register the review on OSF to provide a public record of the review methods and analytic plan and to transparently document the timing and circumstances of the registration. Accordingly, this OSF registration is retrospective with respect to procedures and analyses already undertaken at the time of registration, and prospective with respect to analyses not yet conducted.

Although the OSF registration occurred after analyses had begun, the primary hypotheses and principal analytic approach described here were established before examination of  the meta-analytic results. Any analyses developed after examination of the data or results will be identified as such.
table.description:
Early symptoms of mood, anxiety, and psychotic disorders typically begin during childhood and adolescence, indicating that early detection and potentially prevention of frank illness is possible. Several empirical high-risk paradigms have been developed for identifying individuals prior to onset, but research increasingly suggests that risk factors for a given psychiatric disorder are often nonspecific, meaning that risk for one clinical outcome frequently confers risk for other clinical outcomes as well. These findings have motivated a body of work seeking to identify factors associated with transdiagnostic risk for psychopathology.

The study of task-based functional brain activation is important to understanding the neural substrates of risk and illness. Task-evoked brain activation measured using fMRI can help to identify differences in brain regions and networks associated with neurocognitive, affective, and reward processing, which are frequently impaired in established illness and in risk. In line with this, large-scale meta-analyses have identified common neural circuit alterations associated with adult psychiatric disorders, including alterations of the prefrontal cortex, anterior insula, cingulate cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus. Emerging evidence suggests some of these alterations may be present prior to disorder onset across mood, anxiety, and psychotic disorders. However, evidence comes largely from individual studies focusing on single risk groups and narrative comparison of these studies; no quantitative synthesis of functional brain activation across risk groups and ascertainment paradigms is to our knowledge available.

Several empirical frameworks have been developed for the study of mood, anxiety, and psychosis risk, including familial high-risk approaches (having a close genetic relative with a diagnosis), clinical or symptom-based risk (presenting with attenuated/subthreshold symptoms or clinical features of a full disorder), and temperament based risk (trait-like inhibition common among anxiety disorders). Each of these carries strengths and limitations for the study of psychiatric risk. For example, familial risk studies allow for the study of genetically informed vulnerability in relatively asymptomatic participants, but conventionally focus on a developmental period –– preadolescence –– prior to key illness-related neurodevelopmental changes. Clinical risk paradigms tend to focus on actively symptomatic individuals at the ages of highest risk for incipient disorder onset, but tend to capture complex clinical profiles that complicate inferences about risk-specific vs. transdiagnostic mechanisms. Very few studies have investigated disorder-risk groups and ascertainment paradigms together, leaving unknown whether these conceptual frameworks and methodologies capture common or unique variance in risk.

Thus, current gaps in the literature include a lack of knowledge regarding the extent to which altered functional brain activation varies across (1) risk for different diagnostic outcomes (mood, anxiety psychosis), (2) different risk ascertainment paradigms (family high-risk, clinical/symptom or trait-based risk), and (3) different task domains (cognitive, affective, reward domains). The present protocol seeks to address these limitations through a systematic review and meta-analysis of published studies.
table.research_questions:
What are common neural loci of dysfunction across risk for mood, anxiety, and psychotic disorders? This registration is retrospective, as the primary study results have already been examined. The hypotheses below should therefore not be interpreted as prospectively registered hypotheses; rather, they reflect the hypotheses and theoretical expectations that motivated the review and informed its design. Where relevant, we distinguish these original expectations from interpretations or additional questions that arose after examination of the data.

We hypothesized that task-related brain alterations reported in mood, anxiety, and psychosis risk studies would converge on circuits previously identified in large-scale meta-analyses of established psychopathology, including prefrontal and subcortical networks associated with cognitive, affective, and reward processing.

We expected that task-related brain alterations would be especially prominent in psychosis-risk studies and in those taking a clinical/symptom-based (vs. familial) approach to risk. This was motivated by findings that participants with psychosis and those in more active clinical states tend to show greater functional brain differences than relatively asymptomatic participants with static risk factors. 

We expected that task domains in the represented studies would be associated with activation in both overlapping and distinct neural circuits known to be involved in cognitive, affective, and/or reward processing: cognitive task studies would show activation in prefrontal and parietal areas, affective tasks in amygdala, hippocampal, and anterior insular areas, and reward tasks in prefrontal and insular/striatal areas. 

We did not have hypotheses about the direction of altered brain activation in these groups.

In addition to the primary and secondary expectations of the study, based on knowledge of the field we anticipated several features of the resulting sample. We expected a preponderance of psychosis-risk studies followed by mood-risk and finally anxiety-risk. We expect that familial risk samples would be younger than clinical/symptomatic samples, and that psychosis-risk studies would include more males than females.

table.data_exclusion_criteria:
1.	Full text available

2.	Published in English

3.	Empirical study using task-based functional MRI were included
(3a). Review articles and meta-analyses were excluded
(3b). Other imaging modalities were excluded, including positron emission tomography (PET), single photon emission tomography (SPECT), and magnetoencephalography (MEG)
(3c). Resting state functional MRI studies were excluded

4.	High-risk groups: Procedures must have involved identifying a group at elevated risk for developing a mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder. Operationalization was based on the prior literature; the following were included:
(4a). Familial risk (i.e., first- or second-degree relative with the diagnosis of interest for that study)
(4b). Subclinical symptoms or syndrome (e.g., subclinical depressive or manic symptoms in the absence of lifetime mood disorder; clinical high-risk for psychosis or elevated psychotic experiences)
(4c).	Trait-like presentations (i.e., elevated schizotypy, inhibited temperament or behavioral inhibition in anxiety disorders literature)

5.	High-risk groups: The following operationalizations of risk were excluded:
(5a). Risk defined solely through a dimensional measurement without case-control comparison (e.g., a study of neural engagement associated continuously with subclinical depressive symptoms)
(5b). Risk defined by an individual genetic polymorphism (i.e., 22q11)
(5c).	 Risk defined solely by environmental factors such as trauma exposure
(5d). Animal models of psychopathology

6.	Comparison made between a group at high risk with a control group at lower risk

7.	Reporting of peak voxels for differences between the high-risk and control groups reported in a standardized space (MNI or Talairach)
(7a). Only whole brain analyses were included. 
(7b). Studies which only reported region-of-interest results were excluded. 

8.	Average age of subjects 30 years or lower.

table.search_validation_procedure: During implementation of the search strategy, search results were reviewed to confirm retrieval of relevant studies known to the review team. Search terms were iteratively refined to improve sensitivity and coverage of the relevant literature. No separate formal validation set was established.
table.other_search_strategies: We reviewed the bibliographies of recent systematic reviews covering task-based neuroimaging markers of risk for mood, anxiety, and psychotic disorders to identify studies not captured by our search terms.
table.procedures_to_contact_authors: Authors of the screened studies were not contacted.
table.search_expiration_and_repetition: The primary search was completed December 2022 and was updated July 2026.
table.search_strategy_justification:
PubMed and Web of Science were selected to provide complementary coverage of psychiatric, psychological, neuroimaging, and biomedical literature. The search was constructed to prioritize sensitivity given the heterogeneity in terminology used to describe risk for psychopathology and related phenotypes. Searches therefore combined functional MRI terms with broad terms for mood, anxiety, and psychotic disorders, as well as risk; we included more targeted terms for specific, established risk constructs such as behavioral inhibition, inhibited temperament, and subclinical or psychosis-spectrum experiences. These additional searches were included because relevant studies may characterize participants using these constructs rather than explicitly describing them as being at risk for a psychiatric disorder. Searches were conducted using parallel query structures across PubMed and Web of Science where possible. 

As this review focused on published peer-reviewed studies, a formal grey literature search was not completed. Reference lists of relevant articles and reviews were searched and used to identify additional candidate studies.
table.screening_stages:
Following exclusion of duplicates identified through PubMed and Web of Science, initial screening of the search results was undertaken by two team members. Abstracts for all records were reviewed; the exception was if the record title was unambiguously unrelated to the review topic (e.g., animal or cell culture study, human study with a clear focus on medical disorders such as dementia), in which case the title was used as the determining eligibility criterion. 

Following this first-stage screening, two reviewers completed full-text review.

Ambiguous cases were discussed to reach consensus; a third reviewer was available to resolve diverging conclusions among reviewers if needed. All records which were determined by one reviewer to be included were checked by the second reviewer. 

All screening and full-text review was completed by humans.
table.screened_fields_blinding: Full citations were included in the search results used to screen manuscripts.
table.used_exclusion_criteria:
During screening and full-text review, studies were excluded for the following reasons:

1. Duplicate publication or record
2. Abstract only / full article unavailable
3. Publication not in English
4. Not primary research
5. Did not use functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)
6. Did not include a task-based fMRI paradigm
7. Did not include a high-risk group
8. Did not include a control group
9. Did not report a comparison between the high-risk and control groups

Studies not meeting any exclusion criterion were retained for inclusion.
table.screener_instructions: Screeners were instructed in the eligibility criteria and screening protocol through a series of review-team meetings prior to and during the screening. These meetings included a review and discussion of the inclusion and exclusion criteria, their application to potential studies, and procedures for handling ambiguous cases. Questions or uncertainties arising during screening were discussed among the review team to promote consistent application of the criteria. The screeners had prior experience conducting systematic reviews and applying study eligibility criteria. No separate written screening manual was developed.
table.screening_reliability: The final search included 5,748 records after removal of duplicates. Given the large number of records, half the records were reviewed by one screener and the other half by the second screener (records were alphabetized by the last name of the record's first author). The first 100 records in the second half of the results was screened by both raters to assess agreement; agreement was 100%.
table.screening_reconciliation_procedure: Ambiguous cases were discussed among the reviewer team to reach consensus; a third reviewer was available in the case of divergent conclusions but was not needed. Inclusion/exclusion criteria were reviewed by the review team and the specific point(s) of ambiguity were assessed against these criteria. Relevant literatures including specific publications were reviewed and discussed to support consensus.
table.sample_size:
All studies meeting eligibility criteria were retained in the systematic review; no further sampling of eligible studies was performed.

The primary objective of the meta-analysis was to identify shared regions of altered functional brain activation across populations at risk for psychopathology. We were also interested in identifying patterns of divergence where sufficiently represented in the literature, including across disorder-risk groups and ascertainment paradigms.

Based on methodological recommendations and simulation studies of activation likelihood estimation (ALE), we considered approximately 17 independent experiments to represent the minimum range desirable for adequately powered and robust subgroup analyses, with larger samples preferred (Eickhoff et al., 2016). We anticipated that the final dataset would provide sufficient numbers of experiments for analyses stratified by disorder-risk group (psychosis, mood, and potentially anxiety risk) and ascertainment paradigm (e.g., familial risk, subthreshold symptom/clinical risk), but that analyses crossing these factors (e.g., comparisons of familial and clinical risk groups specifically within the psychosis-risk literature) would likely be underpowered.

We prioritized examining each of the three disorder-risk domains (mood, anxiety, and psychosis) separately where possible, recognizing that the literature on anxiety risk was likely to be less extensive. For the final dataset, the psychosis- and mood-risk analyses (as well as the primary analyses) exceeded the anticipated sample-size benchmark. The anxiety-risk analysis included 11 independent experiments, below the approximately 17 experiment range we had considered desirable. We nevertheless conducted and report this analysis because anxiety constituted an a priori disorder-risk domain of interest and excluding it entirely would omit one of the three major risk domains considered in the review. Results from this analysis are therefore treated as preliminary and interpreted with particular caution given the limited number of experiments and greater potential for individual experiments to influence the resulting convergence pattern.
table.screening_procedure_justification:
The screening procedure was designed to balance sensitivity and methodological rigor with the practical demands of a large and heterogeneous literature. We anticipated identifying a large number of records for several reasons. First, the broader literatures on risk for psychopathology are extensive. Second, the review intentionally spanned multiple disorder-risk literatures, including mood, anxiety, and psychosis risk. Third, risk is operationalized in multiple ways, partly motivating the present review. Some ascertainment paradigms and classification approaches have relatively established conventions (e.g., familial risk across disorders and clinical high-risk criteria in the psychosis literature), whereas others are more heterogeneous (e.g., definitions of subthreshold depressive symptoms). We therefore prioritized sensitivity in the search strategy, with the expectation that this would yield a large number of records requiring screening.

Given an initial pool of approximately 6,000 records and two primary screeners, we did not employ independent duplicate screening of every record at the title/abstract stage. Instead, we used a calibration and quality-assurance procedure that included a series of initial meetings to establish consistent application of the eligibility criteria, independent double-screening of a subset of 100 records, and regular meetings throughout screening to discuss ambiguous cases and identify or prevent potential screener drift. Disagreements and uncertain cases were resolved through discussion and consensus.

We did not blind screeners to study authors or other bibliographic information, as these characteristics were not used in eligibility decisions. Both primary screeners were doctoral-level investigators with substantial familiarity with the relevant psychopathology-risk literatures. Full-text articles retained for inclusion were therefore not independently screened in duplicate by the two primary screeners. As an additional quality-assurance step, however, a third member of the review team reviewed the final set of included studies against the pre-specified inclusion and exclusion criteria.
table.data_management_and_sharing: Search results retrieved from the databases are available in CSV format and will be deposited in the study’s OSF project without embargo when the manuscript is published. Title/abstract and full-text eligibility were assessed as part of the same screening process. We did not maintain a separate log of disagreements between screeners. Final eligibility decisions are included in the CSV. Copyrighted full-text articles will not be shared. We will share a study-level extraction table in .xlsx format containing all extracted information, including citation metadata, sample and demographic characteristics, task and method details, contrasts, and reported peak-voxel coordinates. We will deposit the table in the study’s OSF project and make it publicly available at the time of publication. The files contain information abstracted from published studies, not participant-level data; copyrighted full-text articles will not be redistributed. We will support FAIR reuse by providing structured, openly accessible files with clear variable definitions and source citations, including DOIs when available. We do not plan to use linked-data formats, so we will not claim five-star linked open data.

Data extraction was conducted solely by human reviewers and proceeded in four stages. 

1. Extractors completed a training stage in which the extraction protocol and coding procedures were reviewed and practiced on eligible studies. 
2. A reliability-verification stage was conducted to establish consistency in application of the extraction procedures, with discrepancies discussed and resolved before proceeding. 
3. Data were extracted from the full set of included studies using the established extraction protocol. 
4. During subsequent review of the extracted data, an apparent inconsistency was identified in one dataset. This prompted an additional post-extraction quality-control stage in which a third team member systematically reviewed the extracted data from all included studies against the original reports and confirmed or corrected extracted values and resolved any identified errors or ambiguities.
5. All discrepancies identified during the post-quality control stage were reviewed and verified by the senior author.
table.extractor_instructions: Extractors were instructed to record sample characteristics and demographic information, fMRI task or paradigm details, the contrasts analyzed, and the reported coordinates of peak voxels. These data were entered into the study’s extraction spreadsheet in the associated OSF project.
table.extractor_masking: Extractors were not masked to the research questions, hypotheses, study authors, or other study characteristics. Data extraction was conducted by two research assistants who had not participated in the identification or screening of studies for inclusion. The primary data extracted for the ALE analyses consisted of objectively reported information, including peak activation coordinates and study/sample characteristics. Given the largely objective nature of these data, formal masking was not considered necessary. Extraction accuracy was addressed through the training, reliability-verification, and post-extraction quality-control procedures described above.
table.extraction_reliability: One research assistant completed the initial data extraction. A second reviewer checked the extracted data; extraction was therefore not performed independently by two extractors, and no formal inter-extractor agreement statistic was calculated. After discrepancies were identified, a third quality-control review was completed. The issues identified were reviewed and confirmed by the senior author.
table.extraction_reconciliation_procedure: Data were extracted by one research assistant and reviewed by a second reviewer, so there was no independent dual-extraction round. All extracted data underwent a third quality-control check. Identified discrepancies were reviewed and confirmed by the senior author.
table.extraction_procedure_justification: The extracted variables were selected to characterize the study samples and fMRI paradigms and to support synthesis of reported activation coordinates. Demographic and sample information describe the populations studied; task and contrast details provide context for interpreting the findings; and peak-voxel coordinates are central to the planned coordinate-based synthesis. Given the project’s resources, one research assistant completed the extraction, with review by a second reviewer and a third quality-control check of all extracted data. This provided multiple opportunities to identify errors while avoiding a full independent duplicate extraction. No formal inter-extractor agreement statistic was calculated. Discrepancies identified during quality control were reviewed and confirmed by the senior author.
table.transformations:
Because this registration was completed after data synthesis had begun, the following sections describe the analytic and quality-assessment procedures implemented in the review. Where analyses were developed after examination of the data or results, this is indicated.

1. Coordinate-space transformation. Peak voxel coordinates from eligible whole-brain analyses reported in Talairach space were converted to Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space prior to ALE analysis.

2. Risk-group and ascertainment-paradigm classification. Study-defined samples were classified according to both disorder-risk group and the approach used to ascertain risk.

Disorder-risk classifications were based on the population definitions and methodology reported in each study. Psychosis- and anxiety-risk studies were classified within their respective disorder-risk domains. Studies examining risk for depressive or bipolar disorders were combined into a broader mood-disorder–risk category. At the outset of the review, we were open to examining depressive and bipolar disorder risk separately if supported by the available literature, but anticipated combining these groups if there were insufficient experiments to support separate ALE analyses.

Samples were additionally classified according to the approach used to define risk, which we refer to as ascertainment paradigm. Studies defining risk on the basis of a positive family history of the disorder of interest were classified as familial high-risk (FHR). Studies defining risk based on the presence of subthreshold symptoms, traits, or related phenotypes were classified as phenotypic risk. Within psychosis-risk studies, this category included clinical high-risk, elevated psychotic experiences, and elevated schizotypy samples. Within mood-risk studies, it included subclinical depression, subclinical mania, and depressive/attentional presentations occurring in conjunction with additional risk factors. Within anxiety-risk studies, it included elevated behavioral inhibition or inhibited temperament.

This classification was intended to preserve a distinction between two conceptually different approaches to identifying risk — familial liability versus phenotypic expression of subthreshold symptoms or traits — while providing sufficiently broad categories to permit quantitative synthesis across the heterogeneous definitions and terminology used in the risk literature. This approach also enabled examination of the extent to which patterns of neural alteration were shared or differed across ascertainment paradigms.

3. Task-domain classification. Eligible experiments were classified according to the primary functional domain assessed by the neuroimaging task: cognitive, affective, or reward processing. When a task engaged more than one domain, classification was based on the primary construct or process the task was designed to assess. For example, a task designed to elicit negative affect using timed mental arithmetic and evaluative feedback was classified in the affective domain, whereas a probabilistic reinforcement learning task designed to assess reward processing was classified in the reward domain.

4. Direction of group contrasts. Foci were classified by the direction of the reported group difference: greater activation in the risk group than the comparison group, or lower activation in the risk group than the comparison group. Foci from opposite contrast directions were analyzed separately and were not combined within an ALE analysis
table.missing_data_handling: Information not available in the source reports was recorded as missing or not reported; values were not inferred or imputed. Experiments without the coordinate data required for ALE could not contribute to the quantitative synthesis. Missing descriptive information was retained as unavailable.
table.data_validation: All extracted data underwent review by a second reviewer and a third quality-control check. Discrepancies identified during these checks were reviewed and confirmed by the senior author. For the ALE analyses, coordinates were included only when they came from eligible whole-brain analyses; coordinates reported in Talairach space were converted to MNI space before analysis. Information that could not be determined from the source report was treated as unavailable rather than inferred. Coordinates determined to be outside of gray matter mask were reviewed for accuracy.
table.quality_assessment: To assess the quality of scientific reporting and methodology among the included studies, quality, following prior work we used the Imaging Methodology Quality Assessment Checklist (IMQAC). The IMQAC evaluates studies on the basis of 10 categories, each scored 0 (criteria unfulfilled), 0.5 (criteria partially fulfilled), or 1 (criteria fulfilled), for a total possible score of 10. To fit the context of psychiatric risk studies, we adapted the instrument by adding contextualized definitions and by operationalizing the IMQAC criteria. The adapted version will be included in the supplementary material of the manuscript.
table.synthesis_plan:
Briefly, ALE estimates spatial convergence of brain activation across experiments, which each contribute peak activation voxel coordinates. Within each experiment, peaks are then modeled using a 3-dimensional Gaussian kernel to reflect spatial uncertainty. The kernel is weighted by sample size, with smaller sample sizes resulting in a wider kernel with less intensity, reflecting increased spatial uncertainty, and larger sample sizes resulting in a narrower kernel with greater intensity, reflecting less spatial uncertainty. Gaussians are combined using a voxel-wise maximum to yield a modeled activation map for each experiment. Modeled activation maps are then combined across experiments, yielding a group-level ALE statistic map, in which the voxel-wise ALE value reflects both the number and the spatial specificity of contributing experiments. Assuming spatial independence across experiments, a null distribution is then analytically derived via non-linear histogram integration, allowing for efficient random-effects inference on spatial convergence. Results are corrected for multiple comparisons at the cluster-level using permutation-based cluster-level family-wise error (cFWE) correction. First clusters are identified using a voxel-wise cluster-forming threshold. Then each cluster’s cFWE-corrected p-value is derived by comparing the observed cluster size to a null distribution of cluster sizes from repeated ALE analyses on the same experiments but with spatially randomized foci. 

Following best practices, we used the smaller sample size across at-risk and control samples for Gaussian kernel weighting, set the cluster-forming threshold to 0.001, the number of simulations to create a null distribution of cluster sizes to 5000, and the significance threshold after cFWE correction to 0.05. We did not stratify the meta-analysis by the original modeling set-up (at-risk > control; control > at-risk; non-directional tests involving group), as our aim was to identify areas of altered functional activation, consistent with prior meta-analyses. Follow up analyses examining directional contrasts were also conducted (at-risk > control and control > at-risk).

Our overall meta-analysis was conducted on all included experiments to identify suprathreshold clusters of task-related activation across psychiatric at-risk groups. To unpack group-level cluster findings, we examined which experiments contributed to a cluster, including sample sizes and relative contributions to the cluster’s summed ALE values. Post-hoc analyses then tested for systematic differences between experiments contributing to a cluster and those not contributing. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests compared mean age and percent female. Fisher’s exact tests compared risk status definition, disorder risk domain and task type. Finally, the uncorrected z-score statistical map thresholded at p < .001 was inspected to identify smaller areas of functional difference. Cluster-based thresholds restrict to only larger clusters and may bias results towards larger areas and away from subcortical areas or smaller functional regions.

Eight exploratory meta-analyses were conducted on subsets of experiments grouped by disorder domain (psychosis, mood, anxiety), by risk type (FHR, PR) or by task type (cognitive, affective, reward). Suprathreshold clusters were examined in terms of contributing experiments’ sample size and ALE contribution, and uncorrected z-score statistical maps thresholded at p < .001 were inspected.

The statistical analysis was carried out in R version 4.4.1 (R Project for Statistical Computing) and Python version 3.12.6 (Python Software Foundation). In addition to the Python package Nilearn, fsleyes was used for brain activation displays.
table.criteria_for_conclusions_inference_crite: Conclusions regarding spatial convergence were based on the statistical thresholding and inference criteria outlined in the preceding section, including the prespecified cFWE thresholding procedures. No minimum effect size or other additional quantitative criterion for conclusions was specified. Rather, results were interpreted based on the presence, location, and pattern of statistically significant spatial convergence identified by the ALE analyses, together with the number of experiments contributing to each analysis across disorder risk groups, ascertainment paradigms, and task domains. Those analyses conducted using uncorrected thresholds were interpreted as exploratory and were distinguished from findings surviving pre-specified statistical correction.
table.synthesist_blinding: No blinding was implemented for this study.
table.publication_bias_analyses: We did not conduct a formal statistical test or correction for publication bias. Conventional methods such as funnel plots and Egger’s regression are not directly applicable to ALE, which synthesizes the spatial convergence of reported peak coordinates rather than study-level effect sizes and their precision. We therefore interpret the findings with the possibility of publication and selective-reporting bias in mind.
table.sensitivity_analyses_robustness_checks:
Two sensitivity analyses were conducted for the overall meta-analysis. 

(1) To assess the impact of sample size specifications on modeling spatial uncertainty, the combined sample size of risk and control groups was used to derive Gaussian kernel width. 

(2) To take into account shared variance of overlapping samples, all studies were examined for any statements of overlap between samples. If a study included an explicit statement regarding overlap of the risk sample with another study, the peak coordinates were merged into one experiment, with the sample size taken to be that of the smallest at-risk or control group in the studies.
table.synthesis_procedure_justification:
The analytic procedures were selected to match the available data and the review questions. Peak coordinates reported in Talairach space were converted to MNI space so they could be analyzed in a common coordinate space. We classified studies by disorder-risk group, risk-ascertainment paradigm, task domain, and direction of the group contrast to examine whether spatial convergence differed across these groups and paradigms. 

Classifications were based on the population definitions and task purpose described in each source. Depressive and bipolar risk samples were combined into a broader mood-disorder-risk category because the available experiments did not support separate ALE analyses. Opposite directions of group contrast were analyzed together and separately.

ALE was used because the synthesis was based on reported peak coordinates rather than comparable study-level effect sizes. All extracted data underwent review by a second reviewer and a third quality-control check; discrepancies were reviewed and confirmed by the senior author. Missing information was not inferred or imputed. Experiments without eligible, usable whole-brain coordinates could not contribute to the ALE synthesis.

We conducted ALE analyses across all eligible experiments and within the relevant risk-group and task-domain categories. Inferences were based on the ALE significance criteria used in the analyses: p < 0.05 FWE, exploratory analyses at p < 0.001. We did not blind synthesists to study identity because study reports were needed to classify populations, tasks, and contrasts. No separate inter-synthesist reliability statistic was calculated.
table.synthesis_data_management_and_sharing: Analysis scripts and accompanying documentation will be shared in a public GitHub repository as plain-text source files, with a README describing how to run them. Extracted data, analysis notes, and synthesis outputs will be deposited in the associated OSF project. These will include the extracted data in CSV format and outputs in their native formats (for example, NIfTI files for ALE maps and PDF or PNG files for figures, if applicable). The GitHub repository and OSF project will be publicly accessible at the time of publication, and the OSF project will link to the scripts.

We prioritized examining each of the three disorder-risk domains (mood, anxiety, and psychosis) separately where possible, recognizing that the literature on anxiety risk was likely to be less extensive. For the final dataset, the psychosis- and mood-risk analyses (as well as the primary analyses) exceeded the anticipated sample-size benchmark. The anxiety-risk analysis included 11 independent experiments, below the approximately 17 experiment range we had considered desirable. We nevertheless conducted and report this analysis because anxiety constituted an a priori disorder-risk domain of interest and excluding it entirely would omit one of the three major risk domains considered in the review. Results from this analysis are therefore treated as preliminary and interpreted with particular caution given the limited number of experiments and greater potential for individual experiments to influence the resulting convergence pattern.", "The screening procedure was designed to balance sensitivity and methodological rigor with the practical demands of a large and heterogeneous literature. Third, risk is operationalized in multiple ways, partly motivating the present review. Some ascertainment paradigms and classification approaches have relatively established conventions (e.g., familial risk across disorders and clinical high-risk criteria in the psychosis literature), whereas others are more heterogeneous (e.g., definitions of subthreshold depressive symptoms). Gaussians are combined using a voxel-wise maximum to yield a modeled activation map for each experiment. Modeled activation maps are then combined across experiments, yielding a group-level ALE statistic map, in which the voxel-wise ALE value reflects both the number and the spatial specificity of contributing experiments. Assuming spatial independence across experiments, a null distribution is then analytically derived via non-linear histogram integration, allowing for efficient random-effects inference on spatial convergence. Results are corrected for multiple comparisons at the cluster-level using permutation-based cluster-level family-wise error (cFWE) correction. First clusters are identified using a voxel-wise cluster-forming threshold. report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p > 0.3", "p < .05", "p < .05"), 
    Text = c("Post-hoc testing between the 30 studies contributing to this cluster and 72 not contributing revealed no significant study-level differences in age, percent female, disorder-risk group, ascertainment paradigm, or task domain (all p > 0.3).", 
    "Figure 2: Overall Meta-Analysis: All Disorder-Risk Groups Contributed to Brain Activation Convergence (p < .05, cFWE) (A) One cluster of convergent activation across disorder-specific risk samples was identified in the left inferior and middle frontal gyrus, spanning the ventrolateral and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (k = 319, MNI: x = -46, y = 20, z = 16).", 
    "Figure 3: Clusters of Convergent Brain Activation Across Psychotic Disorder Risk (A), FHR (B) and PR (C) Samples (p < .05 cFWE)."
    )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p > 0.3", Sentence = "Post-hoc testing between the 30 studies contributing to this cluster and 72 not contributing revealed no significant study-level differences in age, percent female, disorder-risk group, ascertainment paradigm, or task domain (all p > 0.3)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. We left out 3 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (3). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer.
